title: 24 Hours in the Life of an Airliner

shots.line: Four forty-five a.m. An airport in the dark.
shots.scene: Ramp at night: jet alone at the gate

shots.line: One jet sits alone at the gate. Cold. Silent. Completely empty.
shots.scene: Empty dark cabin: cold, silent, empty

shots.line: By midnight tonight, this same plane will have flown four flights and carried hundreds of people across thousands of kilometers of sky.
shots.scene: Teaser: 4 flights, hundreds of people

shots.line: Along the way, it will dodge a storm, get struck by lightning, and race the clock on the ground more than once.
shots.scene: Teaser: storm, lightning, race the clock

shots.line: And somewhere in this day hides a moment where the pilots face a split-second decision that can never be taken back. Stay with me, because we'll get there.
shots.scene: Pilot giant face: the split-second decision

shots.line: This is twenty-four hours in the life of an airliner.
shots.scene: Title card over dawn sky

shots.line: Five a.m. The first person to touch the plane isn't a pilot.
shots.scene: Ramp 5 AM: mechanic walks to the jet with a flashlight

shots.line: It's a mechanic, with a flashlight.
shots.scene: Mechanic giant face, flashlight glow

shots.line: Tires. Brakes. Engines. Leaks. Dents. Every panel that should be closed.
shots.scene: Under the wing: mechanic checks, checklist ticks

shots.line: Then a pilot does it all again. A full lap around the plane, before every single flight.
shots.scene: Pilot walks a full lap around the jet

shots.line: Why so careful? Because sometimes, the smallest thing matters most.
shots.scene: Pilot giant face: why so careful?

shots.line: See these little tubes near the nose? They're called pitot tubes. They measure the air rushing past, and that's how the plane knows its airspeed.
shots.scene: Insert: pitot tubes near the nose, airflow

shots.line: In nineteen ninety-six, a jet took off from the Dominican Republic with one of these tubes blocked. Investigators believe the likely culprit was a nest built by tiny wasps while the plane sat on the ground.
shots.scene: 1996: a blocked tube

shots.line: The speed readings went wrong, the crew became confused, and the plane crashed into the ocean.
shots.scene: Airspeed needle goes wild, crash

shots.line: That's why today, when planes sit parked, those tubes get covers with long red ribbons that say: remove before flight.
shots.scene: Insert: covers with red REMOVE BEFORE FLIGHT ribbons

shots.line: Every airliner also has its own identity, painted on the tail and the fuselage: its registration, like a license plate.
shots.scene: Tail close-up: the registration

shots.line: And every plane keeps a detailed record of its life. Every flight, every fault, every repair is written down, so its whole history can be traced, sometimes back to the day it was built.
shots.scene: Logbook: every flight, fault, repair

shots.line: Five fifteen. The fuel truck arrives. But the plane never gets filled to the top.
shots.scene: Ramp 5:15: the fuel truck arrives

shots.line: Fuel is heavy, and carrying extra weight burns even more fuel.
shots.scene: Weight loop: fuel is heavy

shots.line: So every flight gets a carefully calculated amount: enough to reach the destination, enough to divert to another airport if the weather turns bad, plus a final reserve, about thirty minutes of extra flying, that pilots never plan to touch.
shots.scene: Fuel bar splits: trip, alternate, final reserve

shots.line: Five thirty. Here's one you'd never guess. The tires on airliners usually aren't filled with regular air.
shots.scene: Insert: tire close-up, 5:30

shots.line: They're filled with nitrogen. It's dry, so the pressure stays steadier in the freezing cold up high and the heat of a hard landing, and it won't feed a fire if a brake overheats.
shots.scene: Tire full of nitrogen; cold, heat, fire icons

shots.line: Five forty-five. Carts of food roll on board. Those meals were cooked hours ago in a kitchen near the airport, chilled, and packed in.
shots.scene: Ramp 5:45: catering truck lifts its box to the door

shots.line: Up in the sky, they'll be reheated in ovens, not microwaves.
shots.scene: Ovens, not microwaves

shots.line: And whatever they taste like down here, they'll taste blander up there. We'll find out why.
shots.scene: Insert: meal tray, taste fades

shots.line: Six a.m. The pilots climb into the cockpit, load the flight plan, and run their checklists, line by line.
shots.scene: Cockpit at dawn: checklists line by line

shots.line: Outside, the sky starts to glow.
shots.scene: Ramp at sunrise: the sky starts to glow

shots.line: And at the gate, the first strangers of the day are walking toward the door.
shots.scene: Terminal: passengers walking toward the gate

shots.line: Six fifteen. Boarding. Notice something?
shots.scene: Boarding at 6:15: passengers through the terminal to the jet bridge

shots.line: You almost always board on the left side of the plane.
shots.scene: Top view: you board on the LEFT side

shots.line: Nobody is completely sure why.
shots.scene: PAX face: nobody is sure why

shots.line: One popular explanation goes back to ships, which were traditionally loaded from one side, called the port side.
shots.scene: Ships were loaded from the port side

shots.line: Another is simpler: the captain sits on the left, so lining the left side up with the gate is easiest.
shots.scene: Captain sits left, so the left side lines up with the gate

shots.line: Either way, the left door became the standard.
shots.scene: Jet bridge at the left front door: the standard

shots.line: As people find their seats, a low whine starts at the back of the plane.
shots.scene: Cabin filling up; a low whine from the back

shots.line: That's the APU, the auxiliary power unit. It's a small jet engine hidden in the tail. It runs the lights and air conditioning at the gate, and it supplies the blast of air used to start the main engines.
shots.scene: APU: a small jet engine in the tail

shots.line: Six forty. The doors close.
shots.scene: 6:40: doors close

shots.line: A small, powerful tug pushes the plane backward, away from the gate.
shots.scene: Tug pushes the jet back from the gate

shots.line: One engine spins up. Then the other.
shots.scene: Engines spin up, one then the other

shots.line: Six fifty. Lined up on the runway. Takeoff power. The plane starts to roll.
shots.scene: 6:50: lined up on the runway, takeoff power

shots.line: And here's something most passengers never hear about.
shots.scene: Pilot face, something passengers never hear about

shots.line: Before every takeoff, the pilots calculate a special speed called V-one.
shots.scene: V1: a special speed

shots.line: Remember that name. It's going to matter later today.
shots.scene: REMEMBER THAT NAME

shots.line: The nose lifts, the wheels leave the ground,
shots.scene: Rotation, wheels leave the ground

shots.line: and within minutes the plane punches through the clouds into bright sunlight.
shots.scene: Punching through the clouds into sunlight

shots.line: If you've seen our video on why planes cruise at thirty-five thousand feet, you'll know the next part isn't random.
shots.scene: Callback: cruising at 35,000 feet

shots.line: The pilots climb to an altitude worked out for this plane's weight, today's winds, and the traffic around them.
shots.scene: Weight, winds, traffic -> the altitude

shots.line: Up here, the plane is moving at roughly eight hundred kilometers an hour.
shots.scene: Cruise: about 800 km/h

shots.line: Inside, the cabin is pressurized, but not all the way to sea level. It's kept at the pressure you'd feel on a mountain, up to about eight thousand feet.
shots.scene: Pressurized cabin, like a mountain at 8,000 ft

shots.line: That's why your ears pop, and
shots.scene: Ears pop

shots.line: why a sealed bag of chips puffs up like a balloon.
shots.scene: A sealed bag of chips puffs up like a balloon

shots.line: And while you're looking out the window, check the bottom of it. See that tiny hole? Most airliner windows have one.
shots.scene: Window close-up: the tiny hole

shots.line: The window is actually several layers, and that little hole lets the pressure between them balance out, so the outer pane carries the load, and the inner one stays fog-free.
shots.scene: Window layers; the hole balances the pressure

shots.line: Now you'll never stop noticing it.
shots.scene: PAX smirks: never stop noticing it

shots.line: Remember those meals? The dry air and lower pressure dull your sense of taste.
shots.scene: The meals again: dry air and low pressure

shots.line: Studies suggest salty and sweet flavors feel noticeably weaker up here. That's why airline food is often seasoned more heavily than you'd expect.
shots.scene: Taste meters: salty and sweet drop

shots.line: And in the cockpit, there's an unusual rule at many airlines. The two pilots often eat different meals. If one dish turns out to be bad, only one pilot gets sick, and the other can still fly the plane.
shots.scene: Two pilots, two different meals

shots.line: Eight o'clock. The engines throttle back, and the plane glides down in a long, gentle slope.
shots.scene: 8:00: the long, gentle descent

shots.line: Eight twenty. Touchdown. Brakes. Reverse thrust roaring.
shots.scene: 8:20: touchdown, brakes, reverse thrust

shots.line: Flight one is done.
shots.scene: Flight 1 done

shots.line: But for the people on the ground, the real race is just starting. They have less than half an hour.
shots.scene: A stopwatch: less than half an hour

shots.line: Eight twenty-five. The plane rolls up to the gate, and the moment the engines spin down, a crowd swarms it.
shots.scene: 8:25: the jet rolls in, vehicles swarm

shots.line: This is the turnaround. On short routes, it can take as little as twenty-five minutes. Watch how much happens at once.
shots.scene: Top-down: the turnaround, 25 minutes

shots.line: Passengers flow out the front.
shots.scene: Passengers flow out the front

shots.line: Cleaners rush in, grab the trash, check the seat pockets, and wipe down tray tables.
shots.scene: Cleaners rush through the cabin

shots.line: Underneath, baggage handlers unload the last flight's bags and load the next.
shots.scene: Bags out, bags in

shots.line: A catering truck lifts its whole box up to the galley door and swaps the empty carts for full ones.
shots.scene: Catering truck lifts its box, carts swapped

shots.line: The fuel truck connects again. Another truck drains the toilets, and fresh water is pumped in.
shots.scene: Top-down: fuel and water trucks

shots.line: And in the cockpit, the pilots are already preparing the next flight: new flight plan, new weather, new weight numbers.
shots.scene: Cockpit: already preparing the next flight

shots.line: Those weight numbers really matter. Every flight, the crew works out exactly how heavy the plane is, and where that weight sits.
shots.scene: Load sheet: how heavy, and where

shots.line: Too much weight at the front or the back changes how the plane handles. So the passengers, the bags, and the fuel are all added up, and checked against the limits, before the doors ever close.
shots.scene: Balance: weight at the front or back; add it all up

shots.line: Why the rush? Because a plane on the ground earns nothing.
shots.scene: A plane on the ground earns nothing

shots.line: Airlines want their jets in the air as many hours a day as possible. Some jets on short routes fly well over ten hours a day.
shots.scene: 10+ hours a day in the air

shots.line: One late bag, one missing catering cart, one slow fuel truck, and the delay can ripple through every flight for the rest of the day.
shots.scene: Dominoes: one late bag ripples through the day

shots.line: Quick quiz. How much does a jet like this weigh?
shots.scene: QUICK QUIZ

shots.line: For an Airbus A three-twenty, the answer is around forty tonnes empty, and up to nearly eighty tonnes at takeoff, once you add the fuel, the bags, and all of us.
shots.scene: Answer: ~40 t empty, nearly 80 t at takeoff

shots.line: And another question, for you this time. Window seat, or aisle seat? Tell me in the comments. I'll be reading them.
shots.scene: Window seat or aisle seat? Comment

shots.line: Eight fifty. Doors close. Flight two.
shots.scene: 8:50: doors close, flight two

shots.line: Before anyone boards, the flight attendants run their own checks: emergency equipment, oxygen bottles, fire extinguishers, the exits.
shots.scene: Flight attendant runs safety checks

shots.line: Because their main job isn't serving drinks. It's keeping everyone safe.
shots.scene: Crew face: keeping everyone safe

shots.line: Same plane, different passengers, a different city.
shots.scene: Flight 2: same plane, different city

shots.line: This time, the plane flies most of the way on autopilot. And that surprises a lot of people.
shots.scene: Autopilot on

shots.line: Autopilot doesn't mean the pilots relax. They're monitoring the systems, checking the fuel, talking to air traffic control, and constantly asking themselves: what would we do if something went wrong, right now?
shots.scene: Pilots monitor: what would we do if...?

shots.line: Because that's the real job. Not just flying the plane, but being ready for the moment it stops being routine.
shots.scene: Pilot face: ready for when it stops being routine

shots.line: Eleven fifteen. Flight two lands.
shots.scene: 11:15: flight two lands

shots.line: And at noon, something else most passengers never notice: the crew changes.
shots.scene: Noon: crew swap at the gate

shots.line: Pilots and flight attendants have strict legal limits on how long they can work, so a fresh crew can take over the same plane in the middle of the day.
shots.scene: Duty limits

shots.line: The plane keeps going. The people don't.
shots.scene: The plane keeps going

shots.line: Twelve thirty. Flight three is loading. And on the radar, across the route, something is growing. A line of thunderstorms.
shots.scene: 12:30: storms growing on the radar

shots.line: One p.m. Flight three climbs out. The sky ahead is getting darker.
shots.scene: 1:00 PM: flight three climbs toward a darkening sky

shots.line: In the cockpit, the weather radar paints the storm in green, yellow, and red.
shots.scene: Weather radar paints the storm: green, yellow, red

shots.line: Red means heavy rain, and often violent turbulence.
shots.scene: Red: heavy rain, violent turbulence

shots.line: Pilots don't fly through that. They ask air traffic control for a new path and steer around it, sometimes by many kilometers.
shots.scene: Pilots steer around it

shots.line: Near storms, the ride can still get bumpy.
shots.scene: Bumpy ride near the storm

shots.line: But as we covered in our turbulence video, airliners are built to handle at least two and a half times the force of gravity, plus a fifty percent safety margin on top.
shots.scene: Callback: built for 2.5 G + 50% margin

shots.line: The plane can take it. That's why the seatbelt sign matters more for you than for the plane.
shots.scene: The plane can take it; the seatbelt is for you

shots.line: But storms have another trick, around the edges.
shots.scene: Storm edges: another trick

shots.line: Lightning.
shots.scene: LIGHTNING

shots.line: Here's a fact that sounds terrifying. On average, an airliner is struck by lightning roughly once a year.
shots.scene: Roughly once a year per airliner

shots.line: So what happens when it hits? Usually, a loud bang, a bright flash, and then nothing.
shots.scene: Strike! bang, flash, then nothing

shots.line: The plane's skin is built to carry the electricity. The current hits one point, like the nose, races along the outside of the plane, and leaves from another point, like the tail.
shots.scene: Current races along the skin: in at the nose, out at the tail

shots.line: The people inside are protected, a bit like sitting inside a metal cage.
shots.scene: Passengers safe, like inside a metal cage

shots.line: The flight carries on. But after landing, the plane will need an inspection.
shots.scene: The flight carries on

shots.line: Engineers will hunt for tiny burn marks where the lightning went in, and where it came out.
shots.scene: Hunting for burn marks: in and out

shots.line: Two thirty. Out of the storm and back into smooth air.
shots.scene: 2:30: back in smooth air

shots.line: But the storm has slowed everything down at the destination. So air traffic control sends our jet into a holding pattern: a big oval racetrack in the sky, with other planes stacked above and below, each waiting its turn to land.
shots.scene: Holding pattern: racetrack in the sky, planes stacked

shots.line: And remember that extra fuel from this morning? This is exactly what it's for. The pilots circle for fifteen minutes, and the final reserve is still untouched.
shots.scene: The extra fuel is for exactly this; reserve untouched

shots.line: And on the way down, another hazard most passengers never see. Birds.
shots.scene: On the way down: birds

shots.line: Every year, there are thousands of bird strikes in the United States alone. Most happen low, during takeoff and landing, which is exactly where birds fly.
shots.scene: Thousands of bird strikes a year, mostly low

shots.line: Most do little or no damage. Engines are even tested by firing bird-sized objects into them, to prove they can take it.
shots.scene: Engines tested by firing bird-sized objects

shots.line: But a big enough flock can stop an engine.
shots.scene: A big enough flock can stop an engine

shots.line: That's exactly what happened to the jet that landed on the Hudson River in two thousand nine.
shots.scene: Hudson River, 2009

shots.line: Three fifteen. Flight three lands safely, and the mechanics walk straight to the nose.
shots.scene: 3:15: flight three lands

shots.line: They find what they're looking for. Two tiny marks, one where the lightning went in, and one at the tail where it left.
shots.scene: Mechanic at the nose: two tiny marks

shots.line: An inspection, a quick repair, and the plane is cleared to fly again.
shots.scene: Inspection, quick repair, cleared

shots.line: Four p.m. The sun is getting lower, and at the next airport the temperature is dropping fast.
shots.scene: 4:00 PM: sun lower, temperature dropping

shots.line: Flight four is the last flight of the day. And it's the one where that number from this morning, V-one, finally matters.
shots.scene: Flight 4, the last flight: V1 finally matters

ov.text: THE LAST FLIGHT OF THE DAY
